hits: "Chrysostom's sermons never stopped being read. Reformation writers quoted him too. Calvin prized his saying that humility is 'the foundation of our philosophy'. But he thought Chrysostom gave the human will too much power. The Augsburg Confession of 1530 cited him on how the early church shared Communion. And the Communion liturgy that carries his name is still the normal Sunday rite of the Eastern Orthodox churches. The Antiochene way of reading held that a text means what it meant to those who first heard it. Later Western Bible scholars made a similar historical-grammatical method standard. How much they owed to Antioch directly is not clear. The school's own fate was harsher. Theodore of Mopsuestia was condemned at Constantinople in 553, more than a century after his death. Much of his work survives only in Syriac translation, kept safe by the Church of the East."

"Around 1173 a rich merchant of Lyon named Valdes gave away his property. He had parts of Scripture put into the language people actually spoke, and he began preaching in the streets. His confession of faith was wholly orthodox. What he would not do was stop preaching without a license, and in 1184 the bull Ad abolendam condemned him and his followers for exactly that. Driven out of the cities, the movement held on in the Alpine valleys between France and Italy. It lasted through three and a half centuries of on-and-off persecution, with its own traveling ministers and its own books. In 1532 its leaders met the Reformers at Chanforan and threw in with the Reformed churches. So a single line of protest runs from twelfth-century Lyon into the Reformation, though scholars disagree about how unbroken it was."

"The Waldensian church is still here. It joined the Reformed churches at Chanforan in 1532, and it lives on as the Waldensian Evangelical Church, based in the same valleys of Piedmont. It is one of the very few medieval movements condemned by Rome that never died out. It never had to be pieced together from its enemies' files. Its long habit of Scripture in the people's own tongue, and of preaching by lay people, came before the Reformation and then joined it."

"These were scattered communities. The barbes, lay preachers who went on foot, linked them together. They lived through Pope Innocent VIII's call to crusade in 1487, and the Cattaneo crusade that came after it. This thread leads to the Synod of Chanforan in 1532. There the Waldensians formally joined the Reformation."

"They are one of the very few medieval dissenting movements still here. In 1532 the Waldensians of the Alps met at Chanforan in the Angrogna valley and joined the Protestant Reformation. The church that came out of it still exists as the Waldensian Evangelical Church. It is based in the same valleys. The valleys keep the memory alive in place names, in caves and hidden meeting places, and in museums the church runs."

"Wittenberg was a small Saxon university town when one of its theology professors, an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther, wrote 95 theses against the sale of indulgences and sent them to the archbishop of Mainz on 31 October 1517. Tradition also holds that he nailed a copy to the door of the Castle Church, the university's usual notice board for an academic debate — but that detail comes only from an account written decades later, after Luther's death, and historians still disagree over whether it happened. Within a few years a movement had grown around him that reorganized worship, emptied monasteries, and put the Bible, a catechism and a hymnbook into ordinary German households. What that looked like from the pew is documented unusually well. From 1527-28 the Saxon churches sent visitors out to examine parish after parish, and their reports are frank about how little many villagers actually knew. The movement settled its own arguments in writing — the Augsburg Confession of 1530, then the Book of Concord of 1580. And the churches shaped by it spread north and east across Germany and Scandinavia, where they remain."

"The Waldensians had already survived three centuries of suppression as an underground movement of lay preachers when, in 1532, their representatives met at Chanforan in the Alpine valleys of Piedmont and agreed to join the young Reformed churches. And to pay for a new French translation of the Bible, which appeared in 1535 as the Olivétan Bible. It was an unusual graft: an old dissenting tradition became a Reformed church with ministers, confessions and printed books, without letting go of its own memory of the centuries before. That memory was tested repeatedly, most brutally in the Piedmont massacre of Easter 1655, which drew protests from across Protestant Europe and a famous sonnet from John Milton."

"Two established national churches emerged: Denmark-Norway's decisive break in 1536/37, and Sweden's slower path from the 1527 Diet of Västerås to the 1593 Uppsala Synod, which committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. Iceland's Reformation was complete by 1550."

"Sweden's break began at the Diet of Västerås in 1527, when Gustav Vasa seized the church's property, and wasn't completed until the Uppsala Synod of 1593 committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. Denmark-Norway moved faster and harder: Christian III arrested the bishops outright in 1536, and Icelandic resistance ended only in 1550, with the execution of the island's last Catholic bishop."

"In Scandinavia the Reformation arrived from the top down and stayed. Sweden's break began at the Diet of Västerås in 1527, when Gustav Vasa took the church's property and its independence, and was only completed at the Uppsala Synod of 1593, which committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. In Denmark-Norway it came faster and harder. Christian III won a civil war, arrested the bishops outright in 1536, and the church ordinance drawn up with Luther's colleague Johannes Bugenhagen reorganized the churches of Denmark, Norway and Iceland at a stroke. Icelandic resistance ended in 1550 with the execution of the island's last Catholic bishop. What followed everywhere was the long, slow business of translating Bibles and hymnbooks and teaching a rural population its catechism."

"The Reformers read him closely. Calvin quoted him with delight: 'The foundation of our philosophy is humility.' Yet he said Chrysostom gave the human will too much power. In 1530 the Augsburg Confession named him as a witness to how the early church shared Communion."
"Worms and Antwerp, 1525 to 1536. An English scholar in exile who wanted a ploughboy to know the Scriptures, and died at the stake for his books."

"Tyndale was born near the Welsh border and studied at Oxford, then at Cambridge. John Foxe tells of a quarrel with a learned priest. Tyndale said that, if God spared his life, he would make a boy who drives the plow know more of the Scripture than the priest did.

He went abroad to print his New Testament. It was in the press at Cologne in 1525, until an enemy of Luther found out the work. Tyndale moved to Worms and printed it there. A report of 1526 said six thousand copies had been printed.

Copies were smuggled into England. In February 1526 Cardinal Wolsey watched baskets of books burn at St Paul's in London. Tyndale said copies of his own book were among them.

He kept writing in exile. The Obedience of a Christian Man came out in 1528, and in 1530 he printed his version of the five books of Moses. In 1535 an Englishman named Henry Philips won his trust at Antwerp. Philips pointed him out to the officers who seized him.

He was condemned under the emperor's decree. At Vilvoorde in 1536 he was strangled at the stake, and his body was burned. Foxe gives his last words: 'Lord, open the king of England's eyes.'"

"Luther was born at Eisleben in 1483. His father was a poor miner. He became an Augustinian friar and taught theology at Wittenberg.

On 31 October 1517 he wrote to the archbishop of Mainz about the indulgences sold under the archbishop's name. His theses of the same day said the indulgence preachers were in error. A later story says he also nailed the theses to the castle church door. It comes from an account written after his death, and historians still disagree about it.

In June 1520 a papal bull condemned his teaching. In April 1521 he stood before the emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms. He refused to take anything back unless Scripture showed him he was wrong. Then he was hidden at the Wartburg castle. There he began what an 1885 historian called the great work of his life, a German Bible from the original text.

He went on writing for twenty-five years more: sermons, hymns, letters, and in 1529 a Small and a Large Catechism. He died on 18 February 1546."

edge.note: In 1530 the Lutheran side named and condemned the Anabaptists in the Augsburg Confession. It rejects their view that children should not be baptized. It also rejects their rule that a Christian may not serve as a judge or ruler.

edge.note: The Augsburg Confession of 1530 calls on Chrysostom as a witness to how the early church shared Communion. Melanchthon wrote a defense of the Confession, known as the Apology. In it he quotes a saying of Chrysostom. It runs: contrition in the heart, confession in the mouth, humility in the work.
